title: Cheapest order to saw a plank
prompt:
Return the minimum total cost to saw a plank of the given length at every position in cuts, where each saw pass costs the length of the piece being cut.

- 2 <= length <= 10^6; cuts has 0 to 200 distinct integers strictly between 0 and length, in any order.
- Cutting a piece that spans [l, r] at position c costs r - l and leaves pieces [l, c] and [c, r].
- Return a single integer (0 when there are no cuts).
hints: Greedy rules such as "always cut nearest the middle" can be beaten. Instead, ask which cut is made first on a given piece.
Sort the cuts and add 0 and length as endpoints. Let cost[i][j] be the cheapest way to make every cut strictly between points[i] and points[j].
cost[i][j] = (points[j] - points[i]) + min over i < k < j of cost[i][k] + cost[k][j], with cost[i][i+1] = 0. Fill it by increasing gap j - i so shorter intervals are ready first.

solution.explanation: Whichever cut k is made first on the piece between points i and j costs the full piece length, then splits the work into two independent sub-pieces. That gives an interval recurrence over pairs of sorted cut points, filled from short intervals to long ones. The answer is cost[0][m - 1] for the whole plank.

complexity.notes: m is the number of cuts plus two; the work depends on how many cuts there are, not on length. Knuth's optimization can reduce this interval DP to O(m^2).

followUps: How would you also return the order in which to make the cuts?
Why does Knuth's optimization apply here, and how does it narrow the choice of k?
